thread.title: 3 Things Investors Need to Know About Qualcomm's Biggest Business

author: Ashraf Eassa, The Motley Fool
title: 3 Things Investors Need to Know About Qualcomm's Biggest Business
text:
One company that's benefited from the rise of the smartphone has been wireless giant Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM) . Since the launch of the Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) iPhone in June of 2007 -- the product that arguably ignited the ultra-mobile computing revolution -- Qualcomm's revenue is up by quite a bit.
QCOM Revenue (TTM) Chart More QCOM Revenue (TTM) data by YCharts .
Qualcomm profits from the smartphone market in two ways. Firstly, it runs a business called Qualcomm Technology Licensing (QTL), which licenses out and collects royalties on its broad set of wireless technology patents. The company also designs and sells a range of chips into smartphones through its chip business, known as Qualcomm CDMA Technologies (QCT).
Here, I'd like to go over some key basics that Qualcomm shareholders ought to know about QCT.
By the numbers During Qualcomm's most recently ended fiscal year -- that's fiscal year 2017 -- Qualcomm raked in $22.29 billion in revenue. Of that, $16.48 billion (or about 74%) came from QCT. The remainder came from QTL.
Although QCT is Qualcomm's largest business unit by revenue by a large margin, the situation is reversed when we look at the pre-tax earnings of each segment. In fiscal year 2017, QCT generated about $2.75 billion in pre-tax earnings (about 16.7% of revenue), while QTL turned in nearly $5.18 billion (approximately 80.3% of revenue) in pre-tax earnings.
Three individuals holding Qualcomm chips. More Image source: Qualcomm.
It's not hard to understand why QCT isn't anywhere near as profitable as QTL. QTL generates its revenue by licensing out its patent portfolio and collecting royalties on the sales devices that incorporate technologies that rely on QTL's portfolio of patents. That's very high-margin revenue.
QCT, on the other hand, sells chips. Not only does QCT incur substantial operating expenses to develop and market a broad portfolio of products, but those products cost something to build and ship -- in other words, that revenue has significant cost of goods sold associated with it. This ultimately means each dollar of revenue that QCT brings in isn't anywhere near as lucrative as each dollar of revenue that QTL generates.
Qualcomm is trying to boost margins In an investor presentation from January 2018, Qualcomm pointed out that QCT saw significant pre-tax earnings growth during its fiscal year 2017 relative to fiscal year 2016 levels. Per the presentation, QCT pre-tax earnings soared 52% year over year as pre-tax earnings as a percentage of QCT revenue expanded roughly 500 basis points to 17%. Sales grew about 7% year over year.
